profiles.meeting_scenario: At a tertiary hospital's cancer service, a gastrointestinal oncology quality-improvement team is preparing a coordination plan for a retrospective service evaluation on how multidisciplinary team (MDT) care affects time-to-treatment and treatment-plan changes for newly diagnosed colorectal cancer patients over the past 18 months. The meeting is between the colorectal MDT clinical lead and the tumor registry/data coordination lead. Their agenda is to align on the patient list to be pulled, the meaning of key workflow milestones taken from different systems, the format of the weekly progress update, and who will maintain the shared tracking sheet used by surgery, oncology, pathology, and radiology liaisons. The expected outcome is a seemingly clear handoff: the registry lead will assemble the cohort and milestone dates, and the MDT lead will review cases flagged as discussed at MDT and summarize downstream management changes for the service evaluation report.

members.name: Dr. Hannah Mercer
members.role: Colorectal Surgeon and MDT Clinical Lead
members.expertise: Colorectal cancer pathways, MDT decision-making, surgical oncology workflow, service redesign
members.background: Hannah is a consultant colorectal surgeon who has chaired the weekly lower-GI cancer MDT for four years and has led several internal pathway-improvement audits focused on reducing delays from diagnosis to definitive treatment.
members.private_state: She wants the evaluation to show that the MDT meaningfully changes management and speeds coordination, but she is worried that incomplete capture of nuanced clinical discussions will make the MDT look less influential than it is.
hidden_assumptions: If a patient appears on the formal lower-GI MDT agenda, that case counts as an MDT-managed case even if the final recommendation is documented later in clinic correspondence.
The 'date of diagnosis' for pathway timing is the date histology confirms malignancy, because that is when the cancer pathway becomes clinically actionable.
A case is 'complete' for review once the first definitive treatment has started or a documented management decision not to treat has been made.
The shared tracker is a working clinical document that data staff update structurally, but the MDT lead's team remains the de facto owner of interpretation and final status labels.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.role: Tumor Registry and Cancer Data Coordination Lead
members.expertise: Cancer registry abstraction, pathway timestamp extraction, audit dataset preparation, EPR reporting workflows
members.background: Priya manages the hospital's cancer outcomes registry team and routinely coordinates data pulls for national submissions, internal audits, and service evaluations across oncology specialties.
members.private_state: She wants a reproducible dataset that her team can extract without manual case-by-case interpretation, and she is concerned about committing her analysts to open-ended tracker maintenance outside standard registry rules.
hidden_assumptions: An 'MDT case' means there is a completed MDT outcome record in the structured EPR field or approved MDT outcomes database, not merely an agenda listing.
The 'date of diagnosis' should follow registry convention: the earliest date the cancer is established by accepted evidence, which can be imaging or endoscopy if that predates histology.
A case is 'complete' only when the first course of treatment is fully coded in the registry workflow, which may lag behind clinical initiation and excludes watch-and-wait until abstracted.
The shared tracker is owned by the requesting clinical team; registry staff can populate agreed fields for a cut of data but do not continuously maintain live status labels.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an MDT case
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to include patients who 'went through MDT' or were 'MDT-managed.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means any patient presented on the formal lower-GI MDT list, including cases where the recommendation is finalized afterward in clinic notes or consultant correspondence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means only patients with a completed structured MDT outcome entry in the EPR/MDT database that can be reliably abstracted.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both work in an environment where 'MDT-managed' is routine shorthand and usually treated as self-explanatory; because they are discussing coordination rather than study design, neither expects the phrase itself to need unpacking.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on pulling the 'diagnosis date' to calculate time from diagnosis to treatment.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the pathology confirmation date, since she views the cancer diagnosis as operationally real once histology returns.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the registry diagnosis date based on the earliest accepted diagnostic evidence, which may be imaging or endoscopic impression before pathology.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Using a single date field sounds like a settled administrative detail; both assume their institution has one obvious diagnosis date and do not treat it as a concept requiring discussion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Priya will send a list of 'complete cases' for Hannah to review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'complete' means enough clinical follow-through exists to judge the MDT's effect: treatment started, surgery performed, or a documented non-treatment plan such as palliative/supportive management.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'complete' means the registry abstraction cycle has all mandatory first-course treatment fields finalized and coded according to registry rules.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word 'complete' feels like a harmless progress label during coordination, and both are accustomed to using it internally without restating the operational threshold.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'keep the tracker updated' and to use the same spreadsheet across teams.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes Priya's team will continue updating milestone dates and case statuses weekly once the initial tracker is set up, because they control the extractable data fields.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes her team will deliver periodic data exports into the tracker template, while Hannah's clinical coordinator owns ongoing maintenance, interpretation, and manual updates between extracts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Shared trackers are common cross-team artifacts, and the phrase 'keep it updated' sounds collaborative rather than contractual; each assumes the normal division of labor from their own context applies.

turns.inner_thought: I need this evaluation to reflect the actual value of the lower-GI MDT, not just what is cleanly coded. If we don't line up the cohort and milestone dates properly at the outset, we'll end up with a dataset that misses where discussion changed direction or sped things along. I want a practical handoff: Priya's team pulls the cases and dates, then we layer on the clinical interpretation.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time, Priya. What I'd like us to do today is get aligned on the patient list for the last 18 months, the key milestone dates we want in the dataset, and how we'll handle the weekly handoff. The whole point of this evaluation is to show whether MDT care is actually changing management and helping patients move through the pathway.

turns.inner_thought: That's workable as long as we define the fields and keep the process reproducible. I can have my team extract a registry cohort and build a tracker template, but I do not want this turning into an open-ended live maintenance job for the registry analysts. The clinical team will need to own the ongoing interpretation and between-run updates.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. We can pull an 18-month cohort from the registry side. If we settle the fields for the shared tracker and the review cycle today, I can get the analysts started and we can keep the tracker updated in a sensible way across teams.

turns.inner_thought: The cohort has to include everyone who came through the formal lower-GI MDT list, even if the final wording of the recommendation sits in a clinic letter or consultant correspondence afterward. If we narrow this to only the neat structured outcomes, we'll undercount the true MDT-managed workload and it will look as though the MDT had less influence than it really did.
turns.utterance: For the cohort, the key thing for me is that we capture all newly diagnosed colorectal patients who went through MDT. That includes the cases where the plan was refined after the meeting, because they were still MDT-managed in practice.

turns.inner_thought: Fine — I'll anchor that on the MDT-managed cases we can identify through the structured MDT outcome records and the relevant EPR fields. That gives us a defensible, reproducible list. If there are informal or only narrative references elsewhere, Hannah can probably review those later, but my pull needs to be based on what is actually recorded in the approved systems.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll use the MDT-managed flag and the outcome records already in the EPR so the starting list is reproducible, and then we can work from there.

turns.inner_thought: What matters most is the pathology-confirmed diagnosis date, first MDT discussion, and when definitive treatment actually starts. That's what makes the pathway clinically actionable and lets us judge whether MDT input is reducing delay. I don't need an overcomplicated extract at this stage.
turns.utterance: In terms of fields, the essentials for me are diagnosis date, first MDT date, and treatment start. If we have those, we can begin looking at where the delays are and where MDT input may have shifted the pathway.

turns.inner_thought: Those are standard enough. I'll take diagnosis date from the registry timeline using our usual convention, then pull the treatment fields alongside it. That should keep the dataset consistent with other audits and avoid case-by-case debate. She sounds like she wants speed, so I won't get into the weeds unless it becomes a problem.
turns.utterance: Those dates should be straightforward. I can pull diagnosis date directly from the registry timeline and line that up with the treatment fields, so we should have a clean backbone for the review.

turns.inner_thought: If I can get a first tranche of cases where treatment has started or a documented non-treatment decision exists, my fellow and I can review whether the MDT changed intent, sequence, or resectability. I don't need every downstream code finished; I need enough clinical follow-through to assess impact. Next Wednesday gives us something concrete to work against.
turns.utterance: Could you send me a first batch of complete cases by next Wednesday? I'd like to start reviewing where the MDT discussion changed intent, sequencing, or suitability for surgery before we scale up.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, complete cases are the easiest place to start because the abstraction cycle is already finalized there. My analysts can produce those without too much manual chasing, and once we've got that initial set out, we can decide how much broader the pull needs to be. That keeps the workload contained.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's doable. I'll start with complete cases because those are the easiest for the team to finalize quickly, and then we can broaden the pull once you've had a look at the first set.

turns.inner_thought: I want one live spreadsheet that people across surgery, oncology, pathology, and radiology can keep using week by week. Priya's team should be able to keep feeding in the milestone dates and statuses because they control the extractable fields, and my side can add the clinical reading of management change. If this splinters into separate versions, we'll lose track very quickly.
turns.utterance: It would help a lot if the same tracker stayed live each week, rather than us rebuilding versions. I'd like status columns for discussed, decision confirmed, treatment started, and any management change after MDT, so everyone is looking at the same picture and we can keep the tracker updated.

turns.inner_thought: A single spreadsheet is fine so long as it functions as a shared template with periodic refreshes from my team, not a live registry-owned operational tool. We'll populate the standard date fields on our usual reporting run, and the clinical side can maintain whatever manual status interpretation sits between those extracts. That division should be obvious.
turns.utterance: That works for me. My team can populate the standard date fields and refresh the tracker on our usual reporting run, so we can use the same spreadsheet across the groups.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll use my fellow to pick up the cases where the MDT effect is visible in the narrative record rather than a tidy coded outcome. That's exactly where the value of discussion often gets lost, and if we don't review those clinic letters and consultant notes, the report will understate how often MDT-managed cases were actually shaped after the meeting.
turns.utterance: That's helpful. I'll have my fellow review the cases where the MDT recommendation is implicit in the clinic letters, so the evaluation captures the real effect of patients going through MDT rather than only the most obvious entries.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect — that means the clinical team will handle the more interpretive layer while we send the reproducible extract. I'll prepare the initial MDT-managed cohort, include diagnosis and treatment dates, and set up the shared tracker for weekly use. As long as we begin with complete cases, this should stay manageable for my analysts.
turns.utterance: Great. So I'll send the initial complete MDT-managed cohort with diagnosis and treatment dates, and I'll set up the shared tracker so we can use it week by week while you review the management changes.
